translations.caution:
A lay hand missal of the 1945 revision, printed about 1955-56, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its Holy Week is the pre-1955 rite, its sanctoral is not the 1962 sanctoral, and its second and third orations are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

Leaf n1316, ordinary printed p. 1302, under the Common of One or More Supreme Pontiffs and `Prayer`. The facing Latin is the 1962 singular Collect with its martyr alternative intact. This is ordinary numbered matter immediately before, and not part of, excluded pp. 1302a-1302d; no other Supreme-Pontiff row is recovered.

translations.caution:
A pre-1955 lay hand missal, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its rubrics, its seasonal second and third orations, its Holy Week and its sanctoral are not those of 1962. A LITERARY TRANSLATION, CHOSEN AS A VOICE. Caswall, Neale, Aylward and Bute
differ materially over these five texts. The active overlay records the
maintainer's choice of Caswall as the through-line across all five and Irons as
an alternative for the Dies irae; it does not argue that either voice is right.

The English is metrical verse and is not a clause-for-clause rendering. Where the
Latin sets a short strophe Caswall may fold two into one six-line stanza, and the
stanza divisions in the text recorded here are his and not the Missal's. He
renders no Amen and no Alleluia anywhere: every one of these five propers ends in
the Latin with an acclamation that the English simply does not have.

Read at printed pp. 138-142 = leaves n175-n179. The book's Missal section does not reprint this sequence: printed p. 244 directs `For Stabat Mater dolorosa, see page 138.`, and p. 138 heads it `Friday after Passion-Sunday. FEAST OF THE SEVEN DOLOURS OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY. VESPERS.` with the incipit `Stabat Mater dolorosa.`, continued under `MATINS (The same continued.)` at p. 140 and `LAUDS (The same continued.)` at p. 141. The three hours together carry the twenty strophes of the Missal sequence with no doxology added at any break, and the last stanza renders both `Christe, cum sit hinc exire` and `Quando corpus morietur`, which is the Missal's ending and not the Breviary hymn's. translations.text:
At the Cross her station keeping,
Stood the mournful Mother weeping,
Close to Jesus to the last:
Through her heart, his sorrow sharing,
All his bitter anguish bearing,
Now at length the sword had pass’d.

Oh, how sad and sore distress’d
Was that Mother highly blest
Of the sole-begotten One!
Christ above in torment hangs;
She beneath beholds the pangs
Of her dying glorious Son.

Is there one who would not weep,
Whelm’d in miseries so deep
Christ’s dear Mother to behold?
Can the human heart refrain
From partaking in her pain,
In that Mother’s pain untold?

Bruis’d, derided, curs’d, defil’d,
She beheld her tender Child
All with bloody scourges rent;
For the sins of his own nation,
Saw Him hang in desolation,
Till his Spirit forth He sent.

O thou Mother! fount of love!
Touch my spirit from above,
Make my heart with thine accord:
Make me feel as thou hast felt;
Make my soul to glow and melt
With the love of Christ my Lord.

Holy Mother! pierce me through;
In my heart each wound renew
Of my Saviour crucified:
Let me share with thee His pain,
Who for all my sins was slain,
Who for me in torments died.

Let me mingle tears with thee,
Mourning Him who mourn’d for me,
All the days that I may live:
By the Cross with thee to stay;
There with thee to weep and pray;
Is all I ask of thee to give.

Virgin of all virgins best!
Listen to my fond request:
Let me share thy grief divine;
Let me, to my latest breath,
In my body bear the death
Of that dying Son of thine.

Wounded with his every wound,
Steep my soul till it hath swoon’d
In his very blood away;
Be to me, O Virgin, nigh,
Lest in flames I burn and die,
In his awful Judgment day.

Christ, when Thou shalt call me hence,
Be thy Mother my defence,
Be thy Cross my victory;
While my body here decays,
May my soul thy goodness praise,
Safe in Paradise with Thee.

propers.name: Collect
propers.text:
Deus, qui multitudinem gentium beati Pauli Apostoli praedicatione docuisti:
da nobis, quaesumus; ut, cujus commemorationem colimus, ejus apud te
patrocinia sentiamus. Per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, Filium tuum: Qui
tecum vivit et regnat in unitate.

translations.caution:
A pre-1955 lay hand missal, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its rubrics, its seasonal second and third orations, its Holy Week and its sanctoral are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

The 1861 prints one Mass for both Chairs of St Peter. Leaf n546, printed p. 538, heads it `XVIII. St. PETER's CHAIR at ROME, &c.` and rubricates `By omitting the COMM. of St. Prisca +, this Mass serves also for his Chair at Antioch on the 22d February.`, so the 22 February commemoration of St Paul is the `Of St. PAUL` oration printed here. Latin cue `Deus, qui multitudinem.` The Kalendar at leaf n775, printed p. 767, sends 22 February to the same p. 538. A bounded page-image collation confirms the complete target identity. For All Souls this is the first 2-November form only; the second and third forms remain quarantined for substantive wording differences.

translations.text: O God, who by the preaching of blessed Paul the Apostle, didst instruct the multitude of the Gentiles: grant, we beseech thee, that whilst we celebrate his memory, we may find the effects of his prayers. Thro'.

translations.caution:
A lay hand missal of the 1945 revision, printed about 1955-56, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its Holy Week is the pre-1955 rite, its sanctoral is not the 1962 sanctoral, and its second and third orations are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

Leaf n936, printed p. 938, under `Postcommunion` at the end of the Mass of Saints Perpetua and Felicity. The facing Latin is the 1962 slot's prayer, with both saints printed by name in both columns.
translations.source_label: The New Roman Missal in Latin and English, revised edition, by F. X. Lasance and Francis Augustine Walsh (New York: Benziger Brothers, 1945), ca. 1955-56 printing (Internet Archive delivery locator fr-lasance-missal-1937; locator mislabelled)
translations.text: Thou hast filled us, O Lord, with mystic graces and joys: grant, we beseech Thee, that through the prayers of Thy holy Martyrs, Perpetua and Felicitas, we may profit eternally from having in this our time ministered to Thee. Through our Lord.

translations.caution:
A pre-1955 lay hand missal, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its rubrics, its seasonal second and third orations, its Holy Week and its sanctoral are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

The 12 March Mass begins on leaf n570, printed p. 562, headed `XII. St. GREGORY, p. c.`, and its Secret and Postcommunion stand at the head of leaf n571, printed p. 563, under the running head `17th AND 19th MARCH`. The Secret is set with no Latin cue; it answers `Annue nobis, quaesumus`. A bounded page-image collation confirms the complete target identity. For All Souls this is the first 2-November form only; the second and third forms remain quarantined for substantive wording differences.

translations.caution:
A pre-1955 lay hand missal, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its rubrics, its seasonal second and third orations, its Holy Week and its sanctoral are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

Leaf n592, printed p. 584, heads 14 May `XIV. St. BONIFACE, m.` and rubricates `All as in Mass V. p. 470, except COLLECT. Da, quaesumus.` -- so the day prints its own Collect only, and its Secret is Mass V's. Mass V is `Protexisti`, of a Martyr in Paschal time; leaf n480, printed p. 472, prints under it `SECRET. Of a Martyr not a Bishop.` with no name in it, word for word the 1962's `Muneribus nostris, quaesumus Domine`. Boniface is a martyr and not a bishop, and 14 May falls in Paschal time, so that is the form the pointer reaches. Page-image collation confirms that this historical English body answers the complete target Latin identity; publication is limited to the 1861 wording and does not claim that Cummiskey appoints the 1962 celebration.

translations.caution:
A lay hand missal of the 1945 revision, printed about 1955-56, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its Holy Week is the pre-1955 rite, its sanctoral is not the 1962 sanctoral, and its second and third orations are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

Leaf n1316, ordinary printed p. 1302, under the Common of One or More Supreme Pontiffs and `Prayer`. The facing Latin is the 1962 singular Collect with its martyr alternative intact. This is ordinary numbered matter immediately before, and not part of, excluded pp. 1302a-1302d; no other Supreme-Pontiff row is recovered.

Through the same.

translations.caution:
A lay hand missal of the 1945 revision, printed about 1955-56, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its Holy Week is the pre-1955 rite, its sanctoral is not the 1962 sanctoral, and its second and third orations are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

Leaf n1316, ordinary printed p. 1302, under the Common of One or More Supreme Pontiffs and `Prayer`. The facing Latin is the 1962 singular Collect with its martyr alternative intact. This is ordinary numbered matter immediately before, and not part of, excluded pp. 1302a-1302d; no other Supreme-Pontiff row is recovered.

translations.caution:
A pre-1955 lay hand missal, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its rubrics, its seasonal second and third orations, its Holy Week and its sanctoral are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

Leaf n672, printed p. 664, heads 26 September `XXVI. SS. CYPRIAN and JUSTINA, mm.`, rubricates `All as in Mass IX. p. 479, except` a proper Collect, and then names `SECRET, (We bring) and P. Comm.(Praesta.) p. 479` -- addressing the two orations by their opening words on that page. `We bring` is Mass VIII's Secret, on leaf n487, printed p. 479, which carries no name and answers the 1962's `Munera tibi, Domine, nostrae devotionis offerimus` word for word. `Praesta` on the same page carries `N. and N.` and is ledgered untranslated. Page-image collation confirms that this historical English body answers the complete target Latin identity; publication is limited to the 1861 wording and does not claim that Cummiskey appoints the 1962 celebration.

differ materially over these five texts. The active overlay records the
maintainer's choice of Caswall as the through-line across all five and Irons as
an alternative for the Dies irae; it does not argue that either voice is right.

The English is metrical verse and is not a clause-for-clause rendering. Where the
Latin sets a short strophe Caswall may fold two into one six-line stanza, and the
stanza divisions in the text recorded here are his and not the Missal's. He
renders no Amen and no Alleluia anywhere: every one of these five propers ends in
the Latin with an acclamation that the English simply does not have.

Read at printed pp. 241-244 = leaves n278-n281, under `Sequence, Mass for the Dead.` and the incipit `Dies irae dies illa.` Nineteen stanzas against the Missal's nineteen strophes, one for one; the closing `Amen.` is not rendered. This corrected the recovered lane brief and the then-current guidance row, which had misidentified the London edition's contents. The London 1849 prints it, in its Missal section, between the Lauda Sion and the cross-reference to the Stabat Mater. An independent English of this sequence is therefore not needed for coverage; the alternative Irons text below is offered as a choice of voice, not as a gap-filler. translations.text:
Nigher still, and still more nigh
Draws the Day of Prophecy,
Doom’d to melt the earth and sky.

Oh, what trembling there shall be,
When the world its Judge shall see,
Coming in dread majesty!

Hark! the trump, with thrilling tone,
From sepulchral regions lone,
Summons all before the throne:

Time and Death it doth appal,
To see the buried ages all
Rise to answer at the call.

Now the books are open spread;
Now the writing must be read,
Which condemns the quick and dead:

Now, before the Judge severe
Hidden things must all appear;
Nought can pass unpunish’d here.

What shall guilty I then plead?
Who for me will intercede,
When the Saints shall comfort need?

King of dreadful Majesty!
Who dost freely justify!
Fount of Pity, save Thou me!

Recollect, O Love divine!
’Twas for this lost sheep of thine
Thou thy glory didst resign:

Satest wearied seeking me;
Sufferedst upon the Tree:
Let not vain thy labour be.

Judge of Justice, hear my prayer!
Spare me, Lord, in mercy spare!
Ere the Reckoning-day appear.

Lo! thy gracious face I seek;
Shame and grief are on my cheek;
Sighs and tears my sorrow speak.

Thou didst Mary’s guilt forgive;
Didst the dying thief receive;
Hence doth hope within me live.

Worthless are my prayers, I know;
Yet, oh, cause me not to go
Into everlasting woe.

Sever’d from the guilty band,
Make me with thy sheep to stand,
Placing me on thy right hand.

When the curs’d in anguish flee
Into flames of misery;
With the Blest then call Thou me.

Suppliant in the dust I lie;
My heart a cinder, crush’d and dry;
Help me, Lord, when death is nigh!

Full of tears, and full of dread,
Is the day that wakes the dead,
Calling all, with solemn blast,
From the ashes of the past.

Lord of mercy! Jesu blest!
Grant the Faithful light and rest.

translations.text:
Day of Wrath! O day of mourning!
See fulfill’d the prophets’ warning!
Heav’n and earth in ashes burning!
Oh, what fear man’s bosom rendeth
When from Heav’n the Judge descendeth,
On Whose sentence all dependeth!

Wondrous sound the trumpet flingeth,
Through earth’s sepulchres it ringeth,
All before the Throne it bringeth.
Death is struck, and nature quaking,
All creation is awaking,
To its Judge an answer making.

Lo! the Book exactly worded,
Wherein all hath been recorded;
Thence shall judgment be awarded.
When the Judge His seat attaineth,
And each hidden deed arraigneth,
Nothing unavenged remaineth.

What shall I, frail man, be pleading,
Who for me be interceding,
When the just are mercy needing?
King of Majesty tremendous,
Who dost free salvation send us,
Fount of pity, then befriend us!

Think, good Jesu, my salvation
Caused Thy wondrous Incarnation;
Leave me not to reprobation.
Faint and weary Thou hast sought me,
On the Cross of suffering bought me;
Shall such grace be vainly brought me?

Righteous Judge! for sin’s pollution
Grant Thy gift of absolution,
Ere that day of retribution.
Guilty, now I pour my moaning,
All my shame with anguish owning;
Spare, O God, Thy suppliant groaning.

Thou the sinful woman savedst;
Thou the dying thief forgavest;
And to me a hope vouchsafest.
Worthless are my prayers and sighing;
Yet, good Lord, in grace complying,
Rescue me from fires undying.

With Thy favour’d sheep O place me,
Nor among the goats abase me,
But to Thy right hand upraise me.
While the wicked are confounded,
Doom’d to flames of woe unbounded,
Call me with Thy Saints surrounded.

Low I kneel, with heart submission,
See, like ashes, my contrition;
Help me in my last condition.

Ah! that day of tears and mourning!
From the dust of earth returning
Man for judgment must prepare him:
Spare, O God, in mercy spare him!
Lord, all-pitying, Jesu Blest,
Grant them Thine eternal rest.
Amen.

translations.text:
Day of Wrath! O day of mourning!
See fulfill’d the prophets’ warning!
Heav’n and earth in ashes burning!
Oh, what fear man’s bosom rendeth
When from Heav’n the Judge descendeth,
On Whose sentence all dependeth!

Wondrous sound the trumpet flingeth,
Through earth’s sepulchres it ringeth,
All before the Throne it bringeth.
Death is struck, and nature quaking,
All creation is awaking,
To its Judge an answer making.

Lo! the Book exactly worded,
Wherein all hath been recorded;
Thence shall judgment be awarded.
When the Judge His seat attaineth,
And each hidden deed arraigneth,
Nothing unavenged remaineth.

What shall I, frail man, be pleading,
Who for me be interceding,
When the just are mercy needing?
King of Majesty tremendous,
Who dost free salvation send us,
Fount of pity, then befriend us!

Think, good Jesu, my salvation
Caused Thy wondrous Incarnation;
Leave me not to reprobation.
Faint and weary Thou hast sought me,
On the Cross of suffering bought me;
Shall such grace be vainly brought me?

Righteous Judge! for sin’s pollution
Grant Thy gift of absolution,
Ere that day of retribution.
Guilty, now I pour my moaning,
All my shame with anguish owning;
Spare, O God, Thy suppliant groaning.

Thou the sinful woman savedst;
Thou the dying thief forgavest;
And to me a hope vouchsafest.
Worthless are my prayers and sighing;
Yet, good Lord, in grace complying,
Rescue me from fires undying.

With Thy favour’d sheep O place me,
Nor among the goats abase me,
But to Thy right hand upraise me.
While the wicked are confounded,
Doom’d to flames of woe unbounded,
Call me with Thy Saints surrounded.

Low I kneel, with heart submission,
See, like ashes, my contrition;
Help me in my last condition.

Ah! that day of tears and mourning!
From the dust of earth returning
Man for judgment must prepare him:
Spare, O God, in mercy spare him!
Lord, all-pitying, Jesu Blest,
Grant them Thine eternal rest.
Amen.

translations.text:
Nigher still, and still more nigh
Draws the Day of Prophecy,
Doom’d to melt the earth and sky.

Oh, what trembling there shall be,
When the world its Judge shall see,
Coming in dread majesty!

Hark! the trump, with thrilling tone,
From sepulchral regions lone,
Summons all before the throne:

Time and Death it doth appal,
To see the buried ages all
Rise to answer at the call.

Now the books are open spread;
Now the writing must be read,
Which condemns the quick and dead:

Now, before the Judge severe
Hidden things must all appear;
Nought can pass unpunish’d here.

What shall guilty I then plead?
Who for me will intercede,
When the Saints shall comfort need?

King of dreadful Majesty!
Who dost freely justify!
Fount of Pity, save Thou me!

Recollect, O Love divine!
’Twas for this lost sheep of thine
Thou thy glory didst resign:

Satest wearied seeking me;
Sufferedst upon the Tree:
Let not vain thy labour be.

Judge of Justice, hear my prayer!
Spare me, Lord, in mercy spare!
Ere the Reckoning-day appear.

Lo! thy gracious face I seek;
Shame and grief are on my cheek;
Sighs and tears my sorrow speak.

Thou didst Mary’s guilt forgive;
Didst the dying thief receive;
Hence doth hope within me live.

Worthless are my prayers, I know;
Yet, oh, cause me not to go
Into everlasting woe.

Sever’d from the guilty band,
Make me with thy sheep to stand,
Placing me on thy right hand.

When the curs’d in anguish flee
Into flames of misery;
With the Blest then call Thou me.

Suppliant in the dust I lie;
My heart a cinder, crush’d and dry;
Help me, Lord, when death is nigh!

Full of tears, and full of dread,
Is the day that wakes the dead,
Calling all, with solemn blast,
From the ashes of the past.

Lord of mercy! Jesu blest!
Grant the Faithful light and rest.

translations.caution:
A pre-1955 lay hand missal, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its rubrics, its seasonal second and third orations, its Holy Week and its sanctoral are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

Leaf n696, printed p. 688, heads 2 November `II. COMMEM. of the FAITHFUL, departed.` and rubricates `All as in the Mass (Requiem) p. 510. except the Collect, Fidelium, with its Secret and P. COMM, as in the Common Mass. p. 518, and what follows.` The oration stands on leaf n526, printed p. 518, in `The COMMON MASS for the DEAD`, under the sub-heading `For all the Faithful departed.` with the Latin cue `Fidelium.` The conclusion is printed `Who livest.` The 1861 is a pre-1915 printing and keeps one Mass on 2 November, not three; the `For all the Faithful departed` set it points at is the 1962 First Mass's three orations word for word, which is why this row names that form. The witness's `For Brethren, Friends, and Benefactors` set on the same leaves is the 1962 Third Mass's. A bounded page-image collation confirms the complete target identity. For All Souls this is the first 2-November form only; the second and third forms remain quarantined for substantive wording differences.

translations.text:
Day of Wrath! O day of mourning!
See fulfill’d the prophets’ warning!
Heav’n and earth in ashes burning!
Oh, what fear man’s bosom rendeth
When from Heav’n the Judge descendeth,
On Whose sentence all dependeth!

Wondrous sound the trumpet flingeth,
Through earth’s sepulchres it ringeth,
All before the Throne it bringeth.
Death is struck, and nature quaking,
All creation is awaking,
To its Judge an answer making.

Lo! the Book exactly worded,
Wherein all hath been recorded;
Thence shall judgment be awarded.
When the Judge His seat attaineth,
And each hidden deed arraigneth,
Nothing unavenged remaineth.

What shall I, frail man, be pleading,
Who for me be interceding,
When the just are mercy needing?
King of Majesty tremendous,
Who dost free salvation send us,
Fount of pity, then befriend us!

Think, good Jesu, my salvation
Caused Thy wondrous Incarnation;
Leave me not to reprobation.
Faint and weary Thou hast sought me,
On the Cross of suffering bought me;
Shall such grace be vainly brought me?

Righteous Judge! for sin’s pollution
Grant Thy gift of absolution,
Ere that day of retribution.
Guilty, now I pour my moaning,
All my shame with anguish owning;
Spare, O God, Thy suppliant groaning.

Thou the sinful woman savedst;
Thou the dying thief forgavest;
And to me a hope vouchsafest.
Worthless are my prayers and sighing;
Yet, good Lord, in grace complying,
Rescue me from fires undying.

With Thy favour’d sheep O place me,
Nor among the goats abase me,
But to Thy right hand upraise me.
While the wicked are confounded,
Doom’d to flames of woe unbounded,
Call me with Thy Saints surrounded.

Low I kneel, with heart submission,
See, like ashes, my contrition;
Help me in my last condition.

Ah! that day of tears and mourning!
From the dust of earth returning
Man for judgment must prepare him:
Spare, O God, in mercy spare him!
Lord, all-pitying, Jesu Blest,
Grant them Thine eternal rest.
Amen.

translations.text:
Nigher still, and still more nigh
Draws the Day of Prophecy,
Doom’d to melt the earth and sky.

Oh, what trembling there shall be,
When the world its Judge shall see,
Coming in dread majesty!

Hark! the trump, with thrilling tone,
From sepulchral regions lone,
Summons all before the throne:

Time and Death it doth appal,
To see the buried ages all
Rise to answer at the call.

Now the books are open spread;
Now the writing must be read,
Which condemns the quick and dead:

Now, before the Judge severe
Hidden things must all appear;
Nought can pass unpunish’d here.

What shall guilty I then plead?
Who for me will intercede,
When the Saints shall comfort need?

King of dreadful Majesty!
Who dost freely justify!
Fount of Pity, save Thou me!

Recollect, O Love divine!
’Twas for this lost sheep of thine
Thou thy glory didst resign:

Satest wearied seeking me;
Sufferedst upon the Tree:
Let not vain thy labour be.

Judge of Justice, hear my prayer!
Spare me, Lord, in mercy spare!
Ere the Reckoning-day appear.

Lo! thy gracious face I seek;
Shame and grief are on my cheek;
Sighs and tears my sorrow speak.

Thou didst Mary’s guilt forgive;
Didst the dying thief receive;
Hence doth hope within me live.

Worthless are my prayers, I know;
Yet, oh, cause me not to go
Into everlasting woe.

Sever’d from the guilty band,
Make me with thy sheep to stand,
Placing me on thy right hand.

When the curs’d in anguish flee
Into flames of misery;
With the Blest then call Thou me.

Suppliant in the dust I lie;
My heart a cinder, crush’d and dry;
Help me, Lord, when death is nigh!

Full of tears, and full of dread,
Is the day that wakes the dead,
Calling all, with solemn blast,
From the ashes of the past.

Lord of mercy! Jesu blest!
Grant the Faithful light and rest.

translations.caution:
A lay hand missal of the 1945 revision, printed about 1955-56, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its Holy Week is the pre-1955 rite, its sanctoral is not the 1962 sanctoral, and its second and third orations are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

Leaf n1316, ordinary printed p. 1302, under the Common of One or More Supreme Pontiffs and `Prayer`. The facing Latin is the 1962 singular Collect with its martyr alternative intact. This is ordinary numbered matter immediately before, and not part of, excluded pp. 1302a-1302d; no other Supreme-Pontiff row is recovered.

translations.caution:
A lay hand missal of the 1945 revision, printed about 1955-56, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its Holy Week is the pre-1955 rite, its sanctoral is not the 1962 sanctoral, and its second and third orations are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

Leaf n1289, printed p. 1289, running head `NOV. 15-ST. ALBERT THE GREAT`, under `Prayer` in the Mass headed `St. Albert the Great, Bishop, Confessor and Doctor of the Church`. The Latin is the 1962 slot's prayer, with the witness's retained-j orthography and abbreviated conclusion. The page itself prints Albert's name, title and English.

translations.caution:
A pre-1955 lay hand missal, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its rubrics, its seasonal second and third orations, its Holy Week and its sanctoral are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

The 1861 keeps this feast on the Second Sunday after Epiphany, not on the Sunday between 2 and 5 January as the 1962 does. Leaf n104, printed p. 94, heads it `II. SUNDAY after EPIPHANY. The FEAST of the HOLY NAME JESUS.` over the Introit `In nomine Jesu`, and its Kalendar at leaf n774, printed p. 766, prints `Second Sunday after Epiphany- Feast of the most Holy Name of Jesus, d. of II. class 94`. The formulary is the same one, and the Latin cue set before this English is `Deus qui`, which answers the 1962's `Deus, qui Unigenitum`. The day placement is a recension difference and not a difference of text. Page-image collation confirms that this historical English body answers the complete target Latin identity; publication is limited to the 1861 wording and does not claim that Cummiskey appoints the 1962 celebration.

Its artifact manifest records the bounded public-domain 1862 Pustet antecedent, the separate 1962 target, and every editorial transformation; neither witness is represented as owning the projected bytes. The 1962 reading was established on that edition's page images rather than its text layer, cross-read against the Benziger conformed printing. Differences from the antecedent: PLACEMENT, as for the other two orations of this Mass.; 1862 sets a comma after 'creasti' ('qui creasti, et redemisti nos'); 1962 sets none.; 1862 sets no comma after 'Filii tui'; 1962 sets one.; 1862 prints 'coelis' with oe; 1962 prints 'caelis' with ae.; Conclusion: 1862 'Per eumdem Dominum nostrum.'; 1962 'Per eundem Dominum.'; Orthography: 1862 'majestati' with j; 1962 'maiestati' with i.; No difference of any word that the 1862 text layer renders legibly -- but see the notes: one word, 'suscipere', it does not render legibly at all.. Corroboration: None available and none claimed; the 1570 and 1604 predate the 1721 extension. The string 'praedestinationis' does occur in the 1604 at line 15772, but in a different prayer ('beatae praedestinationis liber') and it corroborates nothing here.. Recorded limitation: THIS IS THE WEAKEST ENTRY IN THE LANE AND THE ONE TO RE-CHECK FIRST. The 1862 text layer is visibly degraded across exactly this oration, and three of its marks are reconstructions rather than readings: line 55058 reads 'OMnfpotens setorne Deus?' where I have set 'Omnipotens aeterne Deus,' -- the '?' is almost certainly a comma, but I am inferring it from the 1962 and cannot see it; line 55064 reads 'Jesu Christi. majest&ti' with a full stop before a lower-case word, where I have set a comma; and line 55066 reads 'vultu susrinere digneris' where every other witness reads 'suscipere'. 'Susrinere' is not a Latin word and I have treated it as recogniser damage, which is what the artifact record leads one to expect of this scan, but I want it on the record that I did not READ 'suscipere' in the 1862 -- I inferred it. Also damaged and reconstructed the same way: 'redenristi' (55059) for 'redemisti', 'auod' (55062) for 'quod', 'titulogauded-mus' (55069) for 'titulo gaudeamus'. Those three are unambiguous; 'susrinere' is the one I would want a human to confirm. If leaf = printed page + 85 still holds here, the leaf to open is n464 for printed p. 379. I could not open it: the 1862 page images are remote and the brief forbids downloading. I am NOT rounding this up. The verdict is 'matched' because the prayer is unmistakably the same prayer and every legible word agrees; the confidence is 'medium' because one word of it is not legible in the only 1862 witness I was permitted to use. As printed, the 1962 reads 'Iesu Christi', 'maiestati' and 'nomine Iesu' with i.

ordinary_frame.basis: The source prints both a longer and a shorter form. Each appoints a Lesson and Gradual before a later Epistle and Tract; the longer form appoints five Lessons and their intervening chants. The generic Ordinary frame has no form-sensitive repeated-reading module, and the Order-of-Mass inventory explicitly leaves the later Ember chants unplaced. A specialized frame has not yet been modeled, so every row remains source-ordered while the generic frame is withheld.

A reviewer applying the verdict list literally - 'an added or dropped clause' - would call this variant, and the difference is recorded above in full so that reclassifying it needs no re-reading. propers.text:
Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, adesto magnae pietatis tuae mysteriis, adesto
sacramentis: et ad recreandos novos populos, quos tibi fons baptismatis
parturit, spiritum adoptionis emitte; ut, quod nostrae humilitatis gerendum

Christum, Filium tuum: Qui tecum vivit et regnat in unitate Spiritus Sancti
Deus:

translations.caution:
A pre-1955 lay hand missal, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its rubrics, its seasonal second and third orations, its Holy Week and its sanctoral are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

The longest of the fourteen and the one that took five leaves to read: n331 (p. 323), n332 (p. 324), n333 (p. 325), n334 (p. 326), n335 (p. 327). The 1862 at p. 201 prints the opening prayer `Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, adesto magnae pietatis tuae mysteriis, adesto sacramentis ...` under the heading Benedictio Fontis, word for word as the 1962 index carries it, and continues into the preface `Vere dignum et justum est ...` The 1861's English runs from that prayer through the preface, the exorcism, the blessing of the creature of water, the sinking of the paschal candle and the three oil-and-chrism formulas, in the 1962 index's order and with no clause of the index unanswered. The book's ceremonial rubrics are given in square brackets so they can be stripped; they are the book's own italic directions and not part of the prayer. TWO PRINTER'S ERRORS ARE REPRODUCED, NOT MENDED: `the word by fire` for `et saeculum per ignem` (the type reads `word`, the sense is `world`), and the run-on `Thro'--who is to come`. Page-image collation confirms that this historical English body answers the complete target Latin identity; publication is limited to the 1861 wording and does not claim that Cummiskey appoints the 1962 celebration.

translations.text: O Almighty and eternal God, be present at these mysteries, be present at these sacraments of thy great goodness: and send forth the spirit of thy adoption to regenerate the new people, whom the font of baptism bringeth forth: that what is to be done by the ministry of us thy servants, may be accomplished by the effect of thy power. Thro'. R. Amen. It is truly meet and just, right and available to salvation, to give thee thanks always, and in all places, O holy Lord, almighty Father, and eternal God: who, by thy invisible power, dost wonderfully produce the effects of thy sacraments: and, though we are unworthy to administer such great mysteries, yet, as thou dost not abandon the gifts of thy grace, so thou inclinest the ears of thy goodness even to our prayers. O God, whose spirit in the very beginning of the world moved upon the waters; that even then the nature of water might receive the virtue of sanctification: O God, who by water didst wash away the crimes of a guilty world, and by the overflowing of the deluge didst give us a figure of regeneration; that one and the same element might, in a mystery, be the end of vice, and the origin of virtue: look down, O Lord, on thy Church, and multiply in her thy regenerations, who by the streams of thy abundant grace, fillest thy city with joy, and openest the fonts of baptism all over the world for the renewal of the Gentiles; that by the command of thy majesty it may receive the grace of thy Son from the Holy Ghost. Who, by a secret mixture of his divine virtue, may render this water fruitful for the regeneration of men: to the end that those, who are to be sanctified in the immaculate womb of this divine font, and are to be born again new creatures, may come forth a heavenly offspring; and that all, however, distinguished by age in time, or sex in body, may be brought forth to the same infancy by grace, their spiritual mother. Therefore may all unclean spirits, by thy command, O Lord, depart from hence; may all the malice of diabolical wiles be entirely banished; may no power of the enemy prevail here; let him not fly about to lay his snares: let him not creep in by his secret artifices; let him not corrupt with his infection. May this holy and innocent creature be free from all assaults of the enemy, and purified by the destruction of all his malice. May it become a living fountain, a regenerating water, a purifying stream: that all those, that are to be washed in this saving bath, may obtain, by the efficacy of the Holy Ghost, the grace of a perfect purification. Wherefore I bless thee, O creature of water, by the living + God, by the true + God, by the holy + God; by that God, who in the beginning separated thee by his word from the dry land, and whose spirit moved upon thee. Who made thee flow from the fountain of paradise, and commanded thee to water the whole earth with thy four rivers. Who changing thy bitterness in the desert into sweetness, made thee fit to drink; and produced thee out of a rock to quench the thirst of the people. I + bless thee also by our Lord Jesus Christ, his only Son: who, in Cana of Galilee, changed thee into wine, by a wonderful miracle of his power. Who walked upon thee dry-foot, and was baptized in thee by John in the Jordan. Who made thee flow out of his side, together with his blood, and commanded his disciples that such as believed should be baptized in thee, saying: Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Do thou, O Almighty God, mercifully assist us who observe this commandment: do thou graciously inspire us. Do thou with thy mouth bless these clear waters; that besides their natural virtue of cleansing the body, they may also prove effectual for purifying the soul. May the virtue of the Holy Ghost descend into all the water of this font. And make the whole substance of this water fruitful, and capable of bringing to a new life. Here may the stains of all sin be washed out; here may human nature, created to thy image, and reformed to the honour of its author, be cleansed from the filth of the old man: that all who receive this sacrament of regeneration, may be born again new children of true innocence. Thro'--who is to come to judge the living and the dead, and the word by fire. R. Amen. May this font be sanctified and made fruitful by the oil of salvation for such as are to be born anew in it, unto life everlasting. R. Amen. propers.text:
Victimae paschali laudes immolent Christiani. Agnus redemit oves: Christus
innocens Patri reconciliavit peccatores. Mors et vita duello conflixere
mirando: dux vitae mortuus regnat vivus. Dic nobis, Maria, quid vidisti in
via? Sepulcrum Christi viventis: et gloriam vidi resurgentis. Angelicos
testes, sudarium et vestes. Surrexit Christus spes mea: praecedet vos in
Galilaeam. Scimus Christum surrexisse a mortuis vere: tu nobis, victor Rex,
miserere. Amen. Alleluia.

translations.caution:
A LITERARY TRANSLATION, CHOSEN AS A VOICE. Caswall, Neale, Aylward and Bute
differ materially over these five texts. The active overlay records the
maintainer's choice of Caswall as the through-line across all five and Irons as
an alternative for the Dies irae; it does not argue that either voice is right.

The English is metrical verse and is not a clause-for-clause rendering. Where the
Latin sets a short strophe Caswall may fold two into one six-line stanza, and the
stanza divisions in the text recorded here are his and not the Missal's. He
renders no Amen and no Alleluia anywhere: every one of these five propers ends in
the Latin with an acclamation that the English simply does not have.

Read at Internet Archive item LyraCatholica1849, printed pp. 233-234 = leaves n270-n271, under the heading `Sequence, Easter-Sunday.` and the Latin incipit `Victimae Paschali laudes.` Six English stanzas answer the Missal's eight strophes, the fifth stanza carrying `Sepulcrum Christi viventis` and `Angelicos testes` together. The Missal's closing `Amen. Alleluja.` is not rendered; Caswall prints no acclamation.
translations.source_label: Lyra Catholica: containing all the Breviary and Missal hymns, with others from various sources, translated by Edward Caswall (London: James Burns, 1849)
translations.text:
Forth to the paschal Victim, Christians, bring
Your sacrifice of praise:

The Lamb redeems the sheep;
And Christ, the Sinless One,
Hath to the Father sinners reconcil’d.

Together, Death and Life
In a strange conflict strove;
The Prince of Life, who died,
Now lives and reigns.

What thou sawest, Mary, say,
As thou wentest on the way.

I saw the tomb wherein the Living One had lain;
I saw his glory as He rose again;
Napkin and linen clothes, and Angels twain:
Yea, Christ is risen, my hope, and He
Will go before you into Galilee.

We know that Christ indeed has risen from the grave:
Hail, thou King of Victory!
Have mercy, Lord, and save.

propers.name: Sequence
propers.text:
Victimae paschali laudes immolent Christiani. Agnus redemit oves: Christus
innocens Patri reconciliavit peccatores. Mors et vita duello conflixere
mirando: dux vitae mortuus regnat vivus. Dic nobis, Maria, quid vidisti in
via? Sepulcrum Christi viventis: et gloriam vidi resurgentis. Angelicos
testes, sudarium et vestes. Surrexit Christus spes mea: praecedet vos in
Galilaeam. Scimus Christum surrexisse a mortuis vere: tu nobis, victor Rex,
miserere. Amen. Alleluia.

translations.caution:

translations.text:
Forth to the paschal Victim, Christians, bring
Your sacrifice of praise:

The Lamb redeems the sheep;
And Christ, the Sinless One,
Hath to the Father sinners reconcil’d.

Together, Death and Life
In a strange conflict strove;
The Prince of Life, who died,
Now lives and reigns.

What thou sawest, Mary, say,
As thou wentest on the way.

I saw the tomb wherein the Living One had lain;
I saw his glory as He rose again;
Napkin and linen clothes, and Angels twain:
Yea, Christ is risen, my hope, and He
Will go before you into Galilee.

We know that Christ indeed has risen from the grave:
Hail, thou King of Victory!
Have mercy, Lord, and save.

provenance.provenance_authority: Triptych editorial projection verified by page-image collation against the 1962 target edition
provenance.provenance_evidence: The project-owned projection passage reproduces the retained calendar body hash exactly. Its artifact manifest records the bounded public-domain 1862 Pustet antecedent, the separate 1962 target, and every editorial transformation; neither witness is represented as owning the projected bytes. The 1962 reading was established on that edition's page images rather than its text layer, cross-read against the Benziger conformed printing. Differences from the antecedent: THE 1862 TEXT LAYER READS 'et qui causam' WHERE THE 1962 READS 'et, cui causam'. This is a word, not a point.; 1862 'exultantis' for the 1962 'exsultantis'; 1862 sets no comma after 'et'; 1862 conclusion is the short cue 'Per Dominum.'. Corroboration: Venice 1570 at text-layer lines 43962-43965, whose line 43964 reads 'cut cauſaʒ táti audi) paeſtititti' = 'cui causam tanti gaudii praestitisti'. The Vatican typica 1604 could NOT be used: its Dominica in albis leaf is missing or unreadable in that scan's OCR (searches on 'Quasi modo', 'geniti', 'munera' and 'gaudii' over the whole file return nothing in that stretch).. Recorded limitation: THIS IS THE WEAKEST ENTRY IN THE LANE AND THE ONE MOST LIKELY TO BE WRONG. 'qui' is a real Latin word and reads plausibly, so I cannot tell from the text layer alone whether the 1862 Pustet genuinely prints 'qui' or whether the recogniser turned a 'c' into a 'q'. Against the OCR-error reading: 'cu' is recognised correctly elsewhere on the same leaves (cujus at 43904, 43981, 44009). For it: this scan's pointing is already garbled here ('qusesumus^' at 43797 for 'quaesumus,'). The prayer as a whole is corroborated word for word in the 1862; the disputed relative pronoun is carried by the 1570, not by the 1862. If the reviewer requires that the 1862 alone carry every word of a matched entry, this one does not qualify and should be held for an 1862 page-image check.

propers.name: Sequence
propers.text:
Veni, Sancte Spiritus, et emitte caelitus lucis tuae radium. Veni, pater
pauperum, veni, dator munerum, veni, lumen cordium. Consolator optime,
dulcis hospes animae, dulce refrigerium. In labore requies, in aestu
temperies, in fletu solacium. O lux beatissima, reple cordis intima tuorum
fidelium. Sine tuo numine, nihil est in homine, nihil est innoxium. Lava
quod est sordidum, riga quod est aridum, sana quod est saucium. Flecte quod
est rigidum, fove quod est frigidum, rege quod est devium. Da tuis
fidelibus, in te confidentibus, sacrum septenarium. Da virtutis meritum, da
salutis exitum, da perenne gaudium. Amen. Alleluia.

translations.caution:
A LITERARY TRANSLATION, CHOSEN AS A VOICE. Caswall, Neale, Aylward and Bute
differ materially over these five texts. The active overlay records the
maintainer's choice of Caswall as the through-line across all five and Irons as
an alternative for the Dies irae; it does not argue that either voice is right.

The English is metrical verse and is not a clause-for-clause rendering. Where the
Latin sets a short strophe Caswall may fold two into one six-line stanza, and the
stanza divisions in the text recorded here are his and not the Missal's. He
renders no Amen and no Alleluia anywhere: every one of these five propers ends in
the Latin with an acclamation that the English simply does not have.

Read at printed pp. 234-236 = leaves n271-n273, under `Sequence, Whit-Sunday.` and the incipit `Veni Sancte Spiritus.` Ten stanzas against the Missal's ten strophes, one for one. The Missal's closing `Amen. Alleluja.` is not rendered.

ordinary_frame.basis: The source prints both a longer and a shorter form. Each appoints a Lesson and Alleluia before a later Epistle and Sequence; the longer form appoints five Lessons and its intervening chants. The generic Ordinary frame has no form-sensitive repeated-reading module, and the Order-of-Mass inventory explicitly leaves the later Ember chants unplaced. A specialized frame has not yet been modeled, so every row remains source-ordered while the generic frame is withheld.

provenance.locator: editorial-projection artifact physical lines 83-86; antecedent printed p. 313; text-layer lines 47386-47398 (heading IN FESTO SS. TRINITATIS. at 47359; heading Oratio. at 47386)
provenance.provenance_authority: Triptych editorial projection verified by page-image collation against the 1962 target edition
provenance.provenance_evidence: The project-owned projection passage reproduces the retained calendar body hash exactly. Its artifact manifest records the bounded public-domain 1862 Pustet antecedent, the separate 1962 target, and every editorial transformation; neither witness is represented as owning the projected bytes. The 1962 reading was established on that edition's page images rather than its text layer, cross-read against the Benziger conformed printing. Differences from the antecedent: 1862 sets no comma after famulis tuis; 1862 sets unitatem in lower case where the 1962 capitalises Unitatem; 1862 sets no comma after ut; 1862 spells majestatis and ejusdem where the 1962 spells maiestatis and eiusdem (i/j orthography); 1862 writes the conclusion out (Per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum Filium tuum: Qui tecum vivit et regnat.) where the 1962 prints the short cue Per Dominum. This is the one place in my lane where the antecedent is the longer of the two. Corroboration: not reachable. Neither the 1570 nor the 1604 scan yields the Trinity Sunday formulary to a search over its degraded text, and I will not rest a claim or a negative on such a search; the 1604 does print the votive Mass of the Holy Trinity, but its Oratio there is a different prayer. Recorded limitation: ONE LETTER INFERRED, NOT READ, AND CORROBORATED ONLY INSIDE THE SAME WITNESS. The 1862 text layer at line 47389 reads 'confessi6ne vera fidei', dropping the second element of the ae ligature. I did not repair it silently. The reading verae is supported from within the 1862 itself: the same phrase is recognised as 'verae fidei' at lines 13411 and 99852 and as 'verse fidei' at lines 60993, 92825 and 103272, so the book sets veræ and this one occurrence lost a letter to the scan. Note that 'in confessione vera' is also grammatical Latin, so this is a real inference and not a typo I can wave away, which is why confidence is medium. The 1862 also has 'Mnrpotens' at line 47387 for the ornamental O of Omnipotens. The 1862 reading rests on the text layer alone, and I could reach no page image of it.

The 1962 prints 'Qui vivis et regnas cum Deo Patre in unitate.'; the Corpus Christi printing at p. 317 ends with the short cue only; the votive printing writes it out three words longer, adding the equivalent of 'Spiritus Sancti Deus'. Conclusion length only; within the settled tolerance.; Pointing: 1862 sets a comma after word 5 and after word 14 where the 1962 sets none; the 1962 sets a comma after word 10 where the 1862 sets none; the 1962 sets a semicolon at word 20 where the Corpus Christi printing sets a comma; the 1962 sets a colon at word 28 where both 1862 printings set a full stop.; Ligature/orthography: the 1862 renders the ae-ligature of word 11 as 'se' (the documented OCR of the printed ligature); so, independently, does the 1962 CMAA text layer.; No word of the 1962 Collect is missing from the 1862, and no word of the 1862 Collect (apart from the longer conclusion in the votive printing) is missing from the 1962.. propers.name: Sequence
propers.text:
Lauda, Sion, Salvatorem, lauda ducem et pastorem in hymnis et canticis.
Quantum potes, tantum aude: quia major omni laude, nec laudare sufficis.
Laudis thema specialis, panis vivus et vitalis hodie proponitur. Quem in
sacrae mensa cenae, turbae fratrum duodenae datum non ambigitur. Sit laus
plena, sit sonora, sit jucunda, sit decora mentis jubilatio. Dies enim
solemnis agitur, in qua mensae prima recolitur hujus institutio. In hac
mensa novi Regis, novum Pascha novae legis Phase vetus terminat. Vetustatem
novitas, umbram fugat veritas, noctem lux eliminat. Quod in cena Christus
gessit, faciendum hoc expressit in sui memoriam. Docti sacris institutis,
panem, vinum in salutis consecramus hostiam. Dogma datur Christianis, quod
in carnem transit panis, et vinum in sanguinem. Quod non capis, quod non
vides, animosa firmat fides, praeter rerum ordinem. Sub diversis speciebus,
signis tantum, et non rebus, latent res eximiae. Caro cibus, sanguis potus:
manet tamen Christus totus, sub utraque specie. A sumente non concisus, non
confractus, non divisus: integer accipitur. Sumit unus, sumunt mille:
quantum isti, tantum ille: nec sumptus consumitur. Sumunt boni, sumunt mali:
sorte tamen inaequali, vitae vel interitus. Mors est malis, vita bonis: vide
paris sumptionis quam sit dispar exitus. Fracto demum sacramento, ne
vacilles, sed memento, tantum esse sub fragmento, quantum toto tegitur.
Nulla rei fit scissura: signi tantum fit fractura: qua nec status nec
statura signati minuitur. Ecce panis Angelorum, factus cibus viatorum: vere
panis filiorum, non mittendus canibus. In figuris praesignatur, cum Isaac
immolatur: agnus paschae deputatur: datur manna patribus. Bone Pastor, panis
vere, Jesu, nostri miserere: tu nos pasce, nos tuere: tu nos bona fac videre
in terra viventium. Tu, qui cuncta scis et vales: qui nos pascis hic
mortales: tuos ibi commensales, coheredes et sodales fac sanctorum civium.
Amen. Alleluia.

translations.caution:
A LITERARY TRANSLATION, CHOSEN AS A VOICE. Caswall, Neale, Aylward and Bute
differ materially over these five texts. The active overlay records the
maintainer's choice of Caswall as the through-line across all five and Irons as
an alternative for the Dies irae; it does not argue that either voice is right.

The English is metrical verse and is not a clause-for-clause rendering. Where the
Latin sets a short strophe Caswall may fold two into one six-line stanza, and the
stanza divisions in the text recorded here are his and not the Missal's. He
renders no Amen and no Alleluia anywhere: every one of these five propers ends in
the Latin with an acclamation that the English simply does not have.

Read at printed pp. 236-240 = leaves n273-n277, under `Sequence, Solemnity of Corpus Christi.` and the incipit `Lauda Sion Salvatorem.` Twelve stanzas against the Missal's twenty-four strophes, two for one throughout. The printing sets the bracketed marker `[Ecce panis angelorum.]` at the head of the eleventh stanza, which is the strophe at which the postconciliar shorter form begins. The Missal's closing `Amen. Alleluja.` is not rendered.
translations.source_label: Lyra Catholica: containing all the Breviary and Missal hymns, with others from various sources, translated by Edward Caswall (London: James Burns, 1849)
translations.text:
Sion, lift thy voice, and sing;
Praise thy Saviour and thy King;
Praise with hymns thy Shepherd true:
Strive thy best to praise Him well;
Yet doth He all praise excel;
None can ever reach His due.

See to-day before us laid
The living and life-giving Bread!
Theme for praise and joy profound!
The same which at the sacred board
Was, by our Incarnate Lord,
Giv’n to his Apostles round.

Let the praise be loud and high;
Sweet and tranquil be the joy
Felt to-day in every breast;
On this Festival divine,
Which records the origin
Of the glorious Eucharist.

On this Table of the King,
Our new Paschal offering
Brings to end the olden rite;
Here, for empty shadows fled,
Is Reality instead;
Here, instead of darkness, Light.

His own act, at supper seated,
Christ ordain’d to be repeated,
In His Memory divine;
Wherefore now, with adoration,
We the Host of our salvation
Consecrate from bread and wine.

Hear what holy Church maintaineth,
That the bread its substance changeth
Into Flesh, the wine to Blood.
Doth it pass thy comprehending?
Faith, the law of sight transcending,
Leaps to things not understood.

Here, beneath these signs, are hidden
Priceless things, to sense forbidden;
Signs, not things, are all we see;—
Flesh from bread, and Blood from wine;
Yet is Christ, in either sign,
All entire, confess’d to be.

They too, who of Him partake,
Sever not, nor rend, nor break,
But entire, their Lord receive.
Whether one or thousands eat,
All receive the self-same meat,
Nor the less for others leave.

Both the wicked and the good
Eat of this celestial Food;
But with ends how opposite!
Here ’tis life; and there ’tis death;
The same, yet issuing to each
In a difference infinite.

Nor a single doubt retain,
When they break the Host in twain,
But that in each part remains
What was in the whole before;
Since the simple sign alone
Suffers change in state or form,
The Signified remaining One
And the Same for evermore.

Lo! upon the Altar lies,
Hidden deep from human eyes,
Bread of Angels from the skies,
Made the food of mortal man:
Children’s meat to dogs denied;
In old types foresignified;
In the manna Heav’n-supplied,
Isaac, and the Paschal Lamb.

Jesu! Shepherd of the sheep!
Thou thy flock in safety keep.
Living Bread! thy life supply;
Strengthen us, or else we die;
Fill us with celestial grace:
Thou, who feedest us below!
Source of all we have or know!
Grant that with thy Saints above,
Sitting at the feast of love,
We may see Thee face to face.

provenance.provenance_evidence: The project-owned projection passage reproduces the retained calendar body hash exactly. Its artifact manifest records the bounded public-domain 1862 Pustet antecedent, the separate 1962 target, and every editorial transformation; neither witness is represented as owning the projected bytes. The 1962 reading was established on that edition's page images rather than its text layer, cross-read against the Benziger conformed printing. Differences from the antecedent: 1862 sets no comma after quaesumus; 1962 has 'quaesumus, Domine,'; conclusion identical in both: the short cue 'Per Dominum.'; A GAP, RECORDED NOT REPAIRED: the 1862 layer loses the opening of largitate at a line break. Line 49238 ends 'quae tibi de tua' and line 49239 opens 'gitite deferimus'; the syllable 'lar-' that the printed line ended with is gone and the remnant is misread as 'gitite'.; OCR defect resolved in the 1862 layer, not textual: '§Uscipe' for Suscipe (49237), 'sacrosdhcta' for sacrosancta (49240). Both are degraded-latin OCR and are cited as corroboration only, not as a basis.. Recorded limitation: This is the Quinquagesima case exactly: a word broken across a column break, the visible fragment unambiguous, and two other public-domain witnesses printing the word at the same place. The gap is left visible in the antecedent text above as '[lar]gitate' rather than silently mended. NOTE for a reviewer: the 1570 reads 'conseruatione' where the 1962 and the 1862 and the 1604 all read 'conversatione'; the 1570 is used here only for largitate. Target text is given in the project's calendar rendering: unaccented, ae/oe expanded to two letters, printed line wraps joined, and the typica's i normalised to the project's j where it occurs. The typica itself prints no j in this prayer. That normalisation is the project's standing practice (src/sources/calendars/roman-1962/propers.yaml records it in terms at lines 20439, 43595 and 43622).

A LITERARY TRANSLATION, CHOSEN AS A VOICE. Caswall, Neale, Aylward and Bute
differ materially over these five texts. The active overlay records the
maintainer's choice of Caswall as the through-line across all five and Irons as
an alternative for the Dies irae; it does not argue that either voice is right.

The English is metrical verse and is not a clause-for-clause rendering. Where the
Latin sets a short strophe Caswall may fold two into one six-line stanza, and the
stanza divisions in the text recorded here are his and not the Missal's. He
renders no Amen and no Alleluia anywhere: every one of these five propers ends in
the Latin with an acclamation that the English simply does not have.
translations.label: Lyra Catholica: containing all the Breviary and Missal hymns, with others from various sources, translated by Edward Caswall (London: James Burns, 1849)

translations.caution:
THIS IS HYMNS ANCIENT AND MODERN'S TEXT OF IRONS AND NOT DEMONSTRABLY IRONS'S
OWN. That book's compilers are widely said to have altered what they received;
this lane established no instance of alteration in this hymn and ran no collation
against a printing of Irons's own, because none was located. The claim that this
is Irons's translation rests on the 1889 Historical Companion's attribution, read
on its page image; the claim that it is UNALTERED rests on nothing and is not
made.

Most of the hymn is set under vocal score in this printing, so 22 of its 58 lines
were read syllable by syllable from under the staves. That is the weakest point
of the transcription.
translations.label: Hymns Ancient and Modern, Complete Edition with accompanying tunes (London: printed for the proprietors by William Clowes and Sons), hymn 398, W. J. Irons's English of the Dies irae
